clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder of melanosome transport producing partial albinism with a characteristic silvery-grey sheen to the hair, eyelashes and eyebrows
Three types reflect the causative gene: type 1 (MYO5A) with primary neurological disease, type 2 (RAB27A) with immunodeficiency, and type 3 (MLPH) with isolated pigmentary change
Light microscopy of the hair shaft shows large, irregular clumps of pigment, distinguishing it from Chediak-Higashi syndrome
Type 2 is complicated by uncontrolled T-lymphocyte and macrophage activation causing haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
Type 1 features severe developmental delay, hypotonia and neurological impairment without immune dysfunction
Unlike Chediak-Higashi syndrome, leucocytes do not contain giant granules
The accelerated phase of type 2 is life-threatening and requires prompt immunochemotherapy
Haematopoietic stem cell transplantation is curative for the immunological disease of type 2
reference.pathophysiology: Griscelli syndrome is caused by biallelic variants in genes governing the docking and transfer of melanosomes and cytotoxic granules. MYO5A (type 1) encodes a motor protein required in melanocytes and neurons; RAB27A (type 2) is essential for both melanosome transfer and the exocytosis of cytotoxic granules by lymphocytes and natural killer cells; MLPH (type 3) links the two in melanocytes only. Consequently, all types share defective pigment distribution, while RAB27A loss additionally impairs cytotoxic granule release, predisposing to haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis.
additionalInvestigations: Light microscopy of the hair shaft for large pigment clumps
Molecular genetic testing of MYO5A, RAB27A and MLPH
Natural killer and cytotoxic lymphocyte degranulation assays
Full blood count, ferritin, triglycerides and fibrinogen to detect haemophagocytosis
Bone marrow examination when haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is suspected
redFlags: Fever with cytopenias, organomegaly and hyperferritinaemia indicating the accelerated (haemophagocytic) phase in type 2
Rapidly progressive neurological deterioration in type 1
Signs of central nervous system infiltration during the accelerated phase
reference.prognosis: Type 2 is fatal without treatment of the accelerated phase and definitive haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, which can be curative for the immune disease. Type 1 carries a poor neurological prognosis, whereas type 3 has a benign course limited to pigmentary change.
pitfalls: Confusing it with Chediak-Higashi syndrome despite the absence of giant leucocyte granules
Failing to distinguish the neurological (type 1) from the immunological (type 2) form, which changes management
Delaying treatment of the accelerated phase in type 2
Overlooking the diagnostic hair microscopy findings
management: In type 2, treat the haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis accelerated phase with immunochemotherapy per an HLH protocol, using corticosteroids, etoposide and ciclosporin with intrathecal therapy where there is central nervous system involvement
Proceed to allogeneic haematopoietic stem cell transplantation, the only curative treatment for the immunodeficiency of type 2
Provide supportive care with infection prophylaxis, transfusion support and prompt treatment of intercurrent infection
For type 1, deliver supportive neurodisability care with physiotherapy, antiseizure medication and feeding and developmental support, as there is no immune involvement
Recognise that type 3 is limited to pigmentary change and requires only reassurance
Monitor type 2 for reactivation of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis and for neurological involvement
Offer genetic counselling for autosomal recessive inheritance and targeted family testing of MYO5A, RAB27A or MLPH
